lesson.title: One Company to Rule an Industry: Trusts and the Rise of Monopoly Power
lesson.summary: Through the combined tactics of horizontal and vertical integration, Gilded Age industrialists built legal structures called trusts that let them dominate entire industries, raising fears that they had created dangerous monopolies immune to ordinary market competition.
lesson.body:
By the 1880s, the strategies of horizontal integration and vertical integration had allowed a small number of companies to gain overwhelming control over major American industries. A monopoly exists when a single company controls an entire market for a good or service, facing little or no meaningful competition and gaining the power to set prices largely as it chooses rather than having prices set by open competition. Few Gilded Age companies achieved a truly complete, literal monopoly, but several came remarkably close, including John D. Rockefeller's Standard Oil, which controlled an estimated ninety percent of American oil refining by the early 1880s.

The trust was the specific legal tool that made this level of consolidation possible. In 1882, Rockefeller's lawyer Samuel Dodd designed the Standard Oil Trust, an arrangement in which the stockholders of many formally separate, competing companies transferred their shares to a small board of trustees. Those trustees then ran the entire collection of companies as one coordinated enterprise, even though each company continued to exist on paper as a distinct legal entity, often organized this way specifically to get around state laws that restricted one corporation from directly owning stock in another. Other industries quickly copied the trust structure, and by the late 1880s the term trust had become a general shorthand in American political language for any large business combination that seemed to threaten fair competition, whether or not it used the exact legal form Rockefeller's lawyers had designed.

Trusts and near monopolies changed everyday economic life for ordinary Americans. Farmers who depended on a single dominant railroad to ship their crops had little power to negotiate rates. Consumers who bought kerosene, sugar, or other goods controlled by a trust had few alternative sellers to turn to if prices rose. Small business owners who tried to compete against a trust often found themselves undercut by predatory pricing until they were forced to sell out or fail entirely. These experiences turned trusts into a major political issue, especially in agricultural regions of the South and Midwest and in growing industrial cities.

Public criticism of trusts drew on the broader resentment of robber baron tactics and grew louder through the 1880s, as journalists and reformers began documenting specific cases of trusts using unfair or predatory practices to crush competitors. Ida Tarbell's investigative reporting on Standard Oil, published starting in 1902, became the most famous example of this kind of exposure, though public pressure against trusts had already been building for years before her articles appeared.

By 1890, this growing public concern had become impossible for Congress to ignore. Trusts and monopolies were increasingly seen not just as an economic issue but as a threat to fair competition and to democratic government itself, since the enormous wealth concentrated in a few companies could be used to influence elected officials. This pressure led directly to the passage of the Sherman Antitrust Act in 1890, the first federal law aimed squarely at restraining the kind of business combinations that horizontal and vertical integration had made possible.
